title: Data Brokers & Data Collection Security Checklist
metaDescription: Complete checklist to protect against data brokers collecting and selling your personal information. Remove your data and secure your privacy.
intro: Data brokers collect and sell your personal information without your consent, leading to spam calls, identity theft risks, and privacy violations. This checklist helps you identify what data is being collected, remove your information from broker databases, and protect yourself from future data harvesting.

items.task: Search for yourself on major search engines
items.why: Reveals what personal information is publicly available and indexed by search engines.
items.howTo: Search Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo using your full name in quotes, plus variations with your city, age, or phone number. Document all results showing personal details.

items.task: Check major people search engines for your profile
items.why: People search sites like WhitePages and Spokeo display detailed personal information that data brokers compile and sell.
items.howTo: Visit WhitePages, Spokeo, BeenVerified, PeopleFinder, and Intelius. Search for your name and location to see what profiles exist.

items.task: Audit your social media privacy settings
items.why: Public social media profiles are harvested by data brokers to build comprehensive personal profiles for sale.
items.howTo: Review Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Twitter privacy settings. Set profiles to private and limit public information visibility.

items.task: Check if your data appears in known breaches
items.why: Breached data is often sold to data brokers, making your information more widely available for collection and resale.
items.howTo: Use HaveIBeenPwned to check if your email appears in data breaches. Check multiple email addresses you've used over the years.

items.task: Create a spreadsheet of all data exposures found
items.why: Systematic documentation helps track removal progress and identifies the most critical exposures to address first.
items.howTo: List each site, what information appears, contact methods, and opt-out processes. This becomes your removal action plan.

items.task: Submit opt-out requests to major data brokers
items.why: Major brokers like Acxiom, LexisNexis, and Epsilon supply data to hundreds of smaller sites, so removing from these sources has maximum impact.
items.howTo: Visit opt-out pages for Acxiom, LexisNexis, Epsilon, and Experian. Follow their specific removal processes, which may require phone calls or mailed requests.

items.task: Remove profiles from people search websites
items.why: These sites make your personal information easily searchable and often sell access to more detailed reports about you.
items.howTo: Use each site's opt-out process: WhitePages has an online form, Spokeo requires email verification, BeenVerified needs phone verification. Process takes 1-2 weeks per site.

items.task: Opt out of marketing and mailing lists
items.why: Marketing lists are sold between companies and data brokers, creating new exposure vectors for your personal information.
items.howTo: Register with DMAchoice.org for direct mail opt-out, OptOutPrescreen.com for credit offers, and DoNotCall.gov for telemarketing calls.

items.task: Opt out of address change notification services
items.why: Services that track address changes sell this information to data brokers, making your new location immediately available for purchase.
items.howTo: Contact USPS to limit address forwarding information sharing, and opt out of services like Melissa Data and QAS address verification systems.

items.task: Limit public record accessibility where possible
items.why: Many data brokers source information from public records, which can include property records, voter registrations, and court filings.
items.howTo: Contact your county clerk about address confidentiality programs if available. Consider using a PO Box for public filings and voter registration.

items.why: Many sites don't immediately process removal requests, and some may restore your information from backup sources.
items.howTo: Re-search all sites where you submitted removal requests. If information still appears, resubmit requests and escalate to customer service if needed.

items.task: Set up monthly personal information monitoring
items.why: Data brokers continuously collect new information, so regular monitoring catches new exposures before they spread widely.
items.howTo: Set calendar reminders to Google yourself monthly. Use a privacy-focused browser for unbiased search results. Check 3-5 major people search sites regularly.

items.why: Preventing data collection is more effective than removing data after it's already been collected and distributed.
items.howTo: Use fake names for loyalty programs, provide minimal information in online forms, use disposable emails for non-essential signups, and read privacy policies before sharing data.

items.why: Online tracking feeds data broker profiles with browsing habits, interests, and behavioral patterns that increase your profile's commercial value.
items.howTo: Use a privacy-focused browser for sensitive searches, enable ad blockers, disable third-party cookies, and use VPN services when browsing. Clear cookies regularly.

items.why: Services like DeleteMe and Incogni automate the opt-out process and provide ongoing monitoring, saving significant time and effort.
items.howTo: Compare services like DeleteMe ($129/year) and Incogni ($78/year). These services handle opt-outs and monitor for new exposures automatically.

items.task: Read privacy policies before sharing information
items.why: Many companies sell customer data to brokers through clauses buried in privacy policies that users rarely read.
items.howTo: Look for data sharing clauses before signing up for services. Opt out of data sharing when possible. Avoid services that don't allow opt-outs.

pro_tips: Use different variations of your name when searching - include nicknames, maiden names, and common misspellings that data brokers might have on file.
Keep records of all opt-out confirmations and reference numbers. Many sites require this information if you need to follow up on incomplete removals.
Consider using a Google Voice number for opt-out requests to avoid giving data brokers your real phone number during the removal process.
Data brokers often restore information from backup sources after 6-12 months, so set quarterly reminders to re-check major sites.
Some data brokers require physical mail for opt-out requests - use a PO Box or business address rather than your home address for these requests.
